name: Act of March 2, 1889: the Lower Brule reservation (Royce 704)
citation: Act of March 2, 1889, ch. 405, 25 Stat. 888 (in force by proclamation of February 10, 1890)
nations: Lower Brule Sioux Tribe (Kul Wicasa Oyate)
promises: Section 5 set apart for the Indians receiving rations at the Lower Brule agency a reservation running from Old Fort George west to the Presho county line, south to the forty-fourth degree of latitude, and back to the Missouri at Fort Lookout (Royce).

The Act of March 2, 1889 divided the Great Sioux Reservation into separate reservations; section 21 opened the rest to sale for the benefit of the Sioux, and section 19 kept in force all provisions of the 1868 treaty and the 1877 agreement not in conflict with it (Court of Claims, 105 Ct. Cl. 725).

breaches.what: The Commission found the 1890 survey placed the Lower Brule south line north of the true forty-fourth parallel, leaving 25,968.24 acres of the reservation outside it, which the United States disposed of from 1892 to 1911; it held the Lower Brule entitled to the land's value.

breaches.what: The final order fixed the sum due at $18,818.11 plus interest, $71,747.63 in all, and offset all of it against land purchases for the tribe, so nothing was paid.

landTaken: 25,968.24 acres of this reservation left outside the 1890 survey line (Docket 78, 1956).
compensation: $71,747.63 found due, wholly offset; nothing paid (Docket 78, 1961).
today: In 1946 the Court of Claims declined jurisdiction over a Lower Brule claim for 34,664.62 acres excluded by the same survey because it was first raised more than five years after the jurisdictional act; the ration-charge claim was not made for Lower Brule funds (105 Ct. Cl. 725, case C-531 (22)). The survey-strip taking is counted once, under cession-1889-03-02-sioux.

nationVoice.nation: Lower Brule Sioux Tribe (Kul Wicasa Oyate)
nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says the United States broke up the Great Sioux Reservation by the 1889 Act, splitting the Sicangu between Rosebud and Lower Brule and moving the Lower Brule reservation north.

openQuestions: Same land and taking as the Docket 78 survey-strip finding already recorded under cession-1889-03-02-sioux, so this file is marked sameEventAs that record and counted there.
The Docket 78 acreage (25,968.24) and the 1946 court's figure (34,664.62 acres excluded, 3,763.55 included) differ; the court's figures come from the General Accounting Office report. Not reconciled.
The Docket 78 opinion and final order were opened through the primary record's links and not re-read in full for this file.

plain.promised: The 1889 Act gave the Lower Brule a reservation whose south line was to run along the forty-fourth parallel.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1956 that an 1890 survey left 25,968.24 acres of it outside the line, and the United States disposed of that land.
plain.today: $71,747.63 was found due in 1961 but wholly offset, so nothing was paid. The taking is counted once, under the 1889 Act record.
